newsitem.title: ZAMBIA: Zambian opposition rejects proposed talks with govt.
newsitem.headline: Zambian opposition rejects proposed talks with govt.

text.p: Aid donors' efforts to end the political impasse in Zambia appeared doomed on Friday, with the opposition rejecting proposed talks with the government as a non-starter.

Foreign donors want discussions to start by next week between President Frederick Chiluba's government and a coalition of 12 opposition parties, aimed at easing some of the tension between the rival sides. Bitterness has grown since the government passed a constitutional amendment keeping all real presidential challengers out of last November's general elections.

The donors cut aid to Zambia at the time to pressure Chiluba into withdrawing the new law, but he refused to budge and opposition leaders now accuse the foreign governments of using talks as a pretext to restore their aid programmes.
"The talks are a non-starter. The donors and the government are acting in bad faith," said Rodger Chongwe, chairman of the opposition coalition.
"The donors want to use us as an excuse for giving (President Frederick) Chiluba aid. The talks are nothing but a face-saving device," he told Reuters.
Zambia had been a darling of the donor community, instituting sweeping economic reforms and a massive programme of privatising hundreds of state-owned firms.
Seven opposition parties boycotted the elections after the government changed the constitution to bar some candidates, including former president Kenneth Kaunda, from standing.
Donors have told the government the aid squeeze would be eased at Consultative Group of donors meeting in Paris next month -- provided that the government begins dialogue with the opposition.
The Swedish-based International Institute of Democracy and Electoral Assistance (IDEA) was set to mediate in talks, but said no firm date had been set.
"It is up to the government and the opposition to set the date. The opposition has demands that have to be addressed," an IDEA official said.
Chongwe said the opposition was adamant that donors should maintain the cuts to force the government to call fresh elections.
"They are telling us to forget about the elections, to give it to Chiluba and concentrate on laying a framework for subsequent elections. That is unacceptable," he said.
"They are trying to give Chiluba a pat on the back for selling them the country," he added, referring to the ambitious privatisation programme.
